items.text: SEASON 8 · EPISODE 7 · DRAFT  The main hall · Maya, Kit, Odile and Bram · Level L5 · Advanced support (formulas on request)  The band rehearses on Thursday. The loudspeaker cluster isn’t flown, and somebody has noticed the catwalk.  ⚑ RV-160 / RV-162: nobody goes on the unfinished catwalk or stands under a load; rigging is the rigging contractor’s and is never described as instructions. RV-161: figures illustrative. Some choices run on a clock.

items.title: The Catwalk
items.stakes: The band rehearses on Thursday. The loudspeaker cluster isn't flown — and people are starting to look at an unfinished catwalk.
items.reward: A rehearsal with nobody overhead, and a cluster that goes up in the right order.

objectives.text: Decide when the room is tuned

items.rumor: Nobody goes up for a look.

items.alt: The main hall from the floor: the catwalk overhead with one section behind barrier tape and a NO ACCESS sign; Odile points up; Kit looks up; Maya beside them. Nobody is on the catwalk.

bubbles.text: The band's here Thursday. The lighting crew say they can hang the cluster off the catwalk.

items.caption: Rehearsal on Thursday.

lines.text: I could pop up there for five minutes. Just to see the hang points.
No. Not for five minutes. Not for one.

items.prompt: 08:45. The cluster isn't flown. Odile wants an answer by lunch. What do you do?
items.risk: Someone at height on an unfinished catwalk — or a lost rehearsal.
timeout: Kit wanders toward the catwalk stairs.
Bram stops him at the tape.

hints.text: Who owns the load, the hanging and the access?

options.label: Ask Bram to let Kit up on the catwalk for five minutes to look at the hang points
options.result: Bram: “That section isn't finished or inspected. Nobody goes up.”
options.consequence: A look is still a person at height on an unfinished catwalk.
options.fail: Nobody goes up for a look.

options.label: Find out whose each piece is and where it stands: the register for the cluster's weight, the structural engineer's review date, the rigging contractor's install date — through Bram. Nobody on the catwalk
options.result: By lunch: approval due Monday, flying Tuesday, and a plan for Thursday from the ground.

options.label: Take the lighting crew's offer to hang it off the catwalk with a hoist
options.result: Bram: “Not their scope, not approved, not from an unfinished catwalk.”
options.consequence: The wrong people, the wrong place, the wrong order.

options.label: Cancel Thursday's rehearsal
options.result: The band loses a day it can't get back.
options.consequence: Safe, and more than the problem needs.

items.title: The weight changed.
items.body: The register has the answer — Maya's own line. Addendum 4 added two subwoofers to the cluster: 480 kg became 640 kg, a third heavier. The new weight went to the structural engineer nine days ago and was acknowledged the next morning. Her review of the hang points is due Monday; the rigging contractor won't hang a load that hasn't been approved. Nothing failed. The check is working — on Maya's change.
items.label: Test: how much heavier — and why the wait?

items.sub: Advanced · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Maya_Site and Kit_Site beside a board. No cluster until the rigging contractor hangs it. Tomorrow we ground-stack. The back row is thirty metres from the stack, twenty-two from where the cluster will be. Twenty log of thirty over twenty-two — about two point seven dB quieter at the back. Nudge it up and tell the band it's not the real thing. And nobody on that catwalk. Not for a look, not for a minute.

items.title: The engineer at the window
items.body: In 1872 Washington Roebling, chief engineer of the Brooklyn Bridge, was left disabled by caisson disease after working in the pressurised chambers under the river. For about a decade he followed the work from a window in Brooklyn Heights, through a telescope. His wife, Emily Warren Roebling, carried his instructions to the site, learned the engineering herself, and handled the officials. The bridge opened in 1883.

items.title: Not the real thing.
items.body: For Thursday, Dario's crew can ground-stack two loudspeakers on the deck, placed to the maker's instructions. It works — but it isn't the design. The back row is 30 m from the stack and 22 m from where the cluster will hang: about 2.7 dB quieter, and aimed from the wrong place. And the band's engineer is already asking for a day to ‘tune the room’ on it.
items.label: Test: how much quieter — and why not tune on it?

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #78 · AVERY'S LENS  Know whose it is before you ask  Before you ask for anything overhead, know who owns each part — the load, the hardware, the access — and ask them, in that order.  The cluster wasn't late because someone failed. It was late because the check on Maya's own weight change was doing its job.

items.alt: A plan of the main hall drawn to scale: the stage, the proscenium line, the ground-stack on the deck five metres upstage, the planned cluster three metres in front of the proscenium, and the back row at twenty-five metres. A line from the stack to the back row reads 30 m; a dashed line from the cluster reads 22 m; the heading reads 20 × log10(30 ÷ 22) ≈ 2.7 dB quieter at the back on the stack.
items.caption: Close enough to rehearse. Not close enough to tune.

items.prompt: Tuesday. What does the band rehearse on?
known: ◉ Stack 30 m from the back row
items.risk: A rehearsal system that puts someone overhead.
timeout: Thursday morning: no system on the deck.

hints.text: What gets the band sound without anyone going up?

options.label: A ground-stack on the deck, placed by Dario's crew to the maker's instructions, labelled temporary — the band told what it will and won't sound like
options.result: Two stacks on the deck, strapped and signed off by Dario's lead. The band knows the back is a little quiet.
options.consequence: A stand-in that needs nobody overhead.

options.label: Borrow a lighting truss and fly two loudspeakers from it
options.result: Bram: “That's rigging. Not approved, not their scope.”
options.fail: Anything flown is the rigging contractor's, after approval.

options.label: Turn the stack up 10 dB so the back row can hear
options.result: The front rows get 10 dB more than they need.

options.label: Rehearse with no PA
options.result: The band hears nothing in a hall built for amplified sound.

items.prompt: Thursday, after rehearsal. The band's engineer wants tomorrow to tune the room. What do you say?
unknown: What the room does with the cluster
items.risk: A room EQ'd for a system that won't be there.
timeout: The band's engineer starts EQ'ing anyway.
Wednesday's tuning starts from a mess.

hints.text: Which system will the audience hear?

options.label: Yes — use the stack, it's what we have
options.result: A day of EQ, all of it wrong for the cluster.

options.label: Tuning waits for the flown cluster: approval Monday, the rigging contractor flies it Tuesday with the hall cleared, tuning Wednesday — you're first in the room
options.result: The band's engineer grumbles, then books Wednesday.

options.label: Skip tuning — the design is good
options.result: A design is a prediction. The room gets the last word.

items.alt: The finished main hall: the loudspeaker cluster hanging, finished and approved, above the front of the stage; Kit and Maya stand at the far sides of the room, well clear of it.

bubbles.text: Approved Monday, flown Tuesday, tuned today. And I never went up.
You saw more on the drawings anyway.

items.prompt: I only wanted to see them. Is that really so bad?

options.label: “Wanting to see is fine. Going up is the problem. Ask for the steel drawings and the structural engineer's calc — you'll see more on paper than from up there.”

items.title: +2 subwoofers · cluster 640 kg
items.body: Maya's Addendum 4: two subwoofers added to the main cluster for the opening production. Cluster weight 480 → 640 kg, frame and cables included. Register line 23: sent to the structural engineer; acknowledged the next morning.

items.alt: The main hall; the fire alarm panel on the wall shows ALARM; Marshal Lindqvist points at the ceiling where music is still playing; Maya stares.

bubbles.text: The alarm is sounding. Why is your music still playing?

items.title: NO ACCESS · not inspected
items.body: The tag on the barrier tape, in Bram's handwriting: ‘Section C — decking incomplete, handrail not certified, NOT INSPECTED. No access. — B.’ Dated three weeks ago, re-signed this morning.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  Overhead has three owners: the structural engineer approves the load, the rigging contractor hangs it, the GC controls access to anything unfinished. Your number — the weight — starts their work; change it and the review re-opens (% = part ÷ whole × 100). Meanwhile rehearse from the ground and label it temporary (ΔL = 20·log10(d₂ ÷ d₁)). Tune only the system you’ll keep. Nobody goes up for a look.
REFLECTION (optional)  · When have you mistaken a check doing its job for someone being slow?
